newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu seizes on scandal to push rightist line.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu seizes on scandal to push rightist line.

text.p: Within minutes of winning a new lease on political life, Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu took to the airwaves reaffirming a policy that has all but derailed Middle East peacemaking.

His career having been saved because of lack of evidence in a corruption scandal, the Israeli leader seized the moment to lash out at foes real and perceived who he said would steer him and his backers away from a right-wing course.

His Sunday night speech to the nation, broadcast live in the absence of reporters, targeted his opponents in the media and those on the political left whose peace deals he reluctantly inherited with his election last May.

The scandal had clouded peace efforts already in crisis since Netanyahu broke ground last month on the Har Homa Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, halting peace talks and sparking violence which erupted again on Monday.
As the cloud began to dissipate, the crisis came back into view.

Netanyahu's remarks might well have ended with his admission that he made mistakes and his claim to have been vindicated. But without skipping a beat, he launched instead into a defence of his policies in the face of government opponents.

"They refuse to accept the fact the people voted for us and not for them. They refuse to accept the fact we are building on Har Homa. They refuse to accept our efforts to protect the unity of Jerusalem," Netanyahu said.
"They refuse to accept our vigorous opposition to a Palestinian state. They refuse to accept that we are guarding the Golan and not coming down from it."

The speech fanned the flames of division that still run deep in Israel, 11 months after Netanyahu ousted Nobel peace laureate Shimon Peres by fewer than 30,000 votes on a promise to better protect Israelis from Moslem militant suicide bombers.
The comments also underscored the hugeness of the task facing the United States -- as the key Middle East broker -- reconciling Israeli and Palestinian positions so at odds with each other.

And the remarks came at a pivotal time when the sides are supposed to negotiate further Israeli pullbacks from occupied Arab lands and grapple with the toughest issues on their peace agenda -- Jewish settlers, Arab refugees, borders and Jerusalem.
Palestinian cabinet minister Hanan Ashrawi assailed Netanyahu's speech, telling Reuters: "He is already going on with these main items which is why we do not have a peace process right now."

Even after U.S. presidential envoy Dennis Ross shuttled between the sides last week, albeit overshadowed by the corruption scandal, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters in Washington that much work lay ahead.
Ross did manage to get Israeli and Palestinian security chiefs to meet last week to discuss security cooperation severed since Israel started Har Homa.
And at a conference in Malta last week, Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat did meet Israel's Foreign Minister David Levy for the first high-level contact in weeks.
But the Israeli and Palestinian leaders seemed as much at odds as ever. Arafat accused Israel at the weekend of leading "the whole region into catastrophe".

Netanyahu, asked if peace with Palestinians could be negotiated now that the legal threat against him was lifted, underscored the difficulties when he put the onus on the other side, telling CNN: "If they control terrorism and put a stop to it, the answer is yes."
